title: The One-Thread Illusion: Why Node.js Feels Like Magic Until It Isn't
excerpt: Node.js is not a language, it's a runtime. It's single-threaded, and it's non-blocking. Instead of spinning up a new thread for every incoming request, Node runs one thread with an event loop that fires off slow operations and moves on, handling thousands of concurrent requests without the overhead of thread-per-request models. That's the whole thing Netflix, PayPal, and Uber bet on — and the whole reason it falls apart the moment you ask it to do heavy computation instead of juggling I/O.

title: How I Built a Full-Stack Medspa & Dental Clinic Website with Next.js
excerpt: A behind-the-scenes look at how I designed and built a modern, accessible medspa and dental clinic web platform — from architecture decisions to deployment.
content:
# How I Built a Full-Stack Medspa & Dental Clinic Website with Next.js

When a client in the healthcare space approached me to build their online presence, I knew this wasn't going to be a simple brochure site. They needed appointment booking, service listings, staff profiles, a working contact system, and a design that communicated trust and professionalism — all while being fast and accessible.

This is a breakdown of how I built it.

## The Brief

The client ran both a medspa and a dental clinic under one brand. The site needed to:

- Clearly present services across both verticals
- Allow patients to book appointments online
- Work perfectly on mobile (most of their traffic was mobile)
- Load fast — slow healthcare sites lose patients immediately
- Feel premium without feeling cold

## Stack Decision

I went with my standard production stack:

- **Next.js (App Router)** — for server components, SEO, and routing
- **TypeScript** — typed throughout, no exceptions
- **Tailwind CSS** — rapid UI with consistent design tokens
- **MongoDB + Mongoose** — flexible schema for appointments and content
- **Vercel** — deployment with zero config
- **Resend** — transactional emails for booking confirmations

Next.js App Router was the right call here. The marketing pages (Home, Services, About, Contact) needed to be server-rendered for SEO. The booking flow needed interactivity. App Router lets you mix both naturally — server components for static content, client components where state is needed.

## Architecture Overview

```
/app
  /page.tsx              → Landing page (Server Component)
  /services/page.tsx     → Services listing (Server Component)
  /book/page.tsx         → Booking page (Client Component)
  /api/book/route.ts     → Booking API endpoint
  /api/contact/route.ts  → Contact form endpoint
/components
  /ui                    → Reusable primitives
  /sections              → Page-level sections
/lib
  /db.ts                 → MongoDB connection
  /models                → Mongoose schemas
```

## The Booking System

This was the most critical piece. I built a multi-step booking form:

1. **Select service** — filtered by category (dental vs medspa)
2. **Pick a date and time** — available slots fetched from the database
3. **Patient details** — name, contact, notes
4. **Confirmation** — email sent via Resend

The availability logic queries existing bookings for a given date and returns only open slots. Simple, but it needed to handle edge cases — double bookings, same-minute submissions, timezone issues.

```ts
export async function getAvailableSlots(date: string, serviceId: string) {
  await connectDB();
  const booked = await Booking.find({
    date,
    serviceId,
    status: { $ne: 'cancelled' }
  }).select('time');

  const bookedTimes = booked.map(b => b.time);
  const allSlots = generateTimeSlots('09:00', '17:00', 30);

  return allSlots.filter(slot => !bookedTimes.includes(slot));
}
```

## Design Approach

Healthcare design walks a fine line — it needs to feel warm and approachable without being unprofessional. I used:

- A dark navy and gold palette for the medspa sections
- Clean white and teal for the dental sections
- Large, readable typography (Inter for body, a serif for headings)
- Generous whitespace — nothing cramped
- Real photography where provided; placeholder-aware components where not

Tailwind made it easy to keep the design system consistent across sections without writing a single line of custom CSS.

## Accessibility

Accessibility wasn't an afterthought here. Healthcare sites serve users who may have visual impairments, motor difficulties, or cognitive differences. I made sure:

- All interactive elements were keyboard navigable
- ARIA labels were applied to form fields and buttons
- Color contrast met WCAG AA across all text
- Focus rings were visible and styled (not removed)
- Form errors were announced to screen readers

## Deployment

I deployed to Vercel with environment variables for the MongoDB connection string, Resend API key, and a few feature flags. The build passed first time — one of the benefits of TypeScript catching issues before they reach production.

The site went live in three weeks from first commit to deployment. The client was happy. The booking system worked from day one.

## What I'd Do Differently

If I were starting over, I'd add a proper admin dashboard earlier. Managing bookings through MongoDB Compass works fine during development, but clients eventually need a UI. I ended up building a lightweight admin panel post-launch — it would have been cleaner to scope it from the start.

Other than that, the stack held up. Next.js + MongoDB + Vercel continues to be my go-to for client projects at this scale.

title: What It's Like Being a Self-Taught Dev in Nigeria
excerpt: No bootcamp, no CS degree, just curiosity, GitHub, and a lot of broken builds. Here is my honest story of learning full-stack development from scratch.
content:
# What It's Like Being a Self-Taught Dev in Nigeria

I didn't go to a bootcamp. I don't have a Computer Science degree. What I have is a GitHub account, a lot of broken builds, and years of figuring things out by myself — sometimes at midnight, sometimes with terrible internet, sometimes without knowing if what I was learning was even the right thing to learn.

This is that story.

## How It Started

Like most self-taught developers, I didn't start with a plan. I started with curiosity. I saw a website and wanted to know how it was made. That question led me to HTML, which led me to CSS, which led me to JavaScript, which led me down a rabbit hole I haven't climbed out of — and don't intend to.

Nigeria doesn't have the same infrastructure for self-taught developers that exists in, say, the US or Europe. There are no local meetups in most cities. Mentorship is rare and usually informal. Bootcamps exist but they're expensive relative to local incomes, and the quality varies wildly. If you're learning to code here, you're largely learning alone — with YouTube, documentation, Stack Overflow, and sheer stubbornness as your main tools.

## The Real Challenges

**Internet.** This is the first and most persistent challenge. Downloading npm packages on a slow or unstable connection is an exercise in patience. Running `pnpm install` and watching it hang is a rite of passage. I learned to download documentation offline, cache aggressively, and plan heavy downloads for late nights when bandwidth was cheaper.

**No feedback loop.** When you're learning alone, you don't know what you don't know. I spent months building things the wrong way — deeply nested callback hell, no error handling, no types, no tests — because I had no one to tell me there was a better way. Code review culture doesn't exist when you have no one to review your code.

**Imposter syndrome with extra weight.** Imposter syndrome is universal in this industry. But there's an added layer when you're a self-taught developer in a country where tech is still being taken seriously. You're not just doubting yourself — you're also fighting the external assumption that serious software development happens elsewhere.

## What Actually Worked

**Building things.** Not tutorials. Not courses. Actual projects — things that had to work, things I was embarrassed to ship if they were broken. My first real project was MedCore, a Hospital Management System. It was rough. The code was messy. But I had to solve real problems, and that forced me to actually learn.

**Reading other people's code.** GitHub is a free education. I read open-source Next.js projects, looked at how people structured their APIs, studied TypeScript patterns from real codebases. Reading code taught me things no tutorial did.

**Shipping publicly.** Putting things online — even imperfect things — forced me to care about quality. Someone might see this. That accountability made me a better developer faster than anything else.

**Consistency over intensity.** I didn't learn by doing 12-hour coding marathons. I learned by showing up every day, even when I only had an hour. Compound interest applies to skills too.

## Where I Am Now

I build full-stack web applications — Next.js, TypeScript, MongoDB, Vercel — for clients and for myself. I've built a hospital management system, a dental clinic platform, a medspa site, a school management app, and I'm currently working on a pharmacy inventory SaaS.

None of that came from a degree or a bootcamp. It came from building things, breaking things, reading documentation at midnight, and refusing to stop.

## To Other Self-Taught Devs in Nigeria

You are not behind. The path you're on is harder in some ways and more honest in others. Nobody handed you a curriculum — you built one. Nobody gave you a cohort — you found your own people online. That resourcefulness is a skill too, and it will serve you long after you've forgotten the syntax of whatever framework is trending this month.

Keep building. Keep shipping. The work is the credential.

title: Converting a Vanilla JS App to a Next.js PWA
excerpt: The exact steps I took to turn Eve Circles from a plain HTML/JS project into a fully installable Progressive Web App with offline support and Vercel Analytics.
content:
# Converting a Vanilla JS App to a Next.js PWA Eve Circles started as a plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript project — the kind of thing you build when you just want to ship something fast without worrying about framework overhead. It worked. But it had limits: no offline support, no installability, no analytics, and a codebase that was starting to resist further development. I decided to migrate it to Next.js and turn it into a proper PWA. Here's exactly what that process looked like. ## Why Migrate at All? Vanilla JS projects are great for getting started, but they don't scale well. As Eve Circles grew: - Adding new pages meant manually updating navigation everywhere - There was no component reuse — I was copying HTML blocks - No TypeScript meant bugs caught only at runtime - No service worker meant users got nothing when offline - Deployment was manual — no CI, no preview URLs Next.js solved all of these. The PWA layer added installability and offline resilience. ## Step 1: Scaffold the Next.js Project ```bash pnpm create next-app@latest eve-circles --typescript --tailwind --app cd eve-circles ``` I chose the App Router from the start — no point migrating to Pages Router when App Router is the future. ## Step 2: Migrate the HTML Structure to Components I went through the original HTML file and identified repeating patterns — the header, the navigation, cards, modals — and turned each into a React component. The original: ```html
Home About Circles
``` Became: ```tsx // components/Navbar.tsx export function Navbar() { return (
Home About Circles
); } ``` This sounds tedious but it took less than a day. The repetitive parts — the parts that made the vanilla codebase painful — became the most satisfying to componentize. ## Step 3: Migrate the JavaScript Logic Vanilla JS event listeners, DOM manipulation, and fetch calls all moved into React. The key mental shift: instead of querying the DOM and mutating it, I hold state and let React render the result. Before: ```js document.getElementById('join-btn').addEventListener('click', () => { document.getElementById('modal').classList.add('open'); }); ``` After: ```tsx const [modalOpen, setModalOpen] = useState(false); {modalOpen && setModalOpen(false)} />} ``` ## Step 4: Add the PWA Layer I used `next-pwa` to handle the service worker: ```bash pnpm add next-pwa ``` ```js // next.config.js const withPWA = require('next-pwa')({ dest: 'public', disable: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development', register: true, skipWaiting: true, }); module.exports = withPWA({ // your next config }); ``` Then I created the web app manifest: ```json // public/manifest.json { "name": "Eve Circles", "short_name": "EveCircles", "description": "Connect, share, and grow in your circles.", "start_url": "/", "display": "standalone", "background_color": "#0f0f0f", "theme_color": "#7c3aed", "icons": [ { "src": "/icons/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" }, { "src": "/icons/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" } ] } ``` And linked it in the root layout: ```tsx // app/layout.tsx export const metadata: Metadata = { manifest: '/manifest.json', themeColor: '#7c3aed', }; ``` ## Step 5: Offline Support `next-pwa` handles caching automatically with Workbox under the hood. By default it caches: - All static assets (JS, CSS, fonts, images) - Pages visited while online Users who'd visited the app before could now open it with no internet connection and see the last cached state. For Eve Circles, this was a significant UX improvement. ## Step 6: Vercel Analytics One `pnpm add @vercel/analytics` and three lines of code later: ```tsx import { Analytics } from '@vercel/analytics/react'; export default function RootLayout({ children }) { return ( {children} ); } ``` I now had real page view data, without cookies, without GDPR headaches. ## Results - **Lighthouse PWA score:** 100 - **Performance score:** 97 (up from ~71 on the vanilla version) - **Installable** on Android and desktop Chrome - **Offline-capable** for previously visited pages - **Codebase:** Maintainable, typed, and ready for new features The migration took about a week of focused evenings. Every hour was worth it.
